What a vector is

PDF page 1

On the board

12.2 Vectors.

Vector: a quantity that describes a magnitude and a direction.

Represent vectors using arrows, denoted by a bold letter: v⃗\vec vv, v\mathbf{v}v.

Arrows: length indicates magnitude, direction by arrow.

v⃗=AB→\vec v = \overrightarrow{AB}v=AB,   u⃗=AC→\vec u = \overrightarrow{AC}u=AC,   r⃗=BA→\vec r = \overrightarrow{BA}r=BA.

AAA is the initial point, or tail. BBB is the terminal point, also called the head or tip.

Two vectors are equal (or equivalent) when they have same magnitude and same direction.

The zero vector 0⃗\vec 00 has magnitude zero and no direction.

A number such as a mass or a temperature is one piece of information. A vector is two: how much, and which way. That is why an arrow is the natural picture, since an arrow has a length and points somewhere.

Where the arrow is drawn is not part of the vector. Slide it anywhere without turning or stretching it and it is still the same vector, which is what the two blue arrows marked u⃗=v⃗\vec u = \vec vu=v show. BA→\overrightarrow{BA}BA has the same length as AB→\overrightarrow{AB}AB but the opposite direction, so r⃗\vec rr and v⃗\vec vv are not equal.

A note on notation: your textbook prints vectors in bold, v\mathbf{v}v. Bold is hard to write by hand, so on the board and on paper the same vector is written v⃗\vec vv. These pages use the arrow, as the board does.

Adding vectors

PDF pages 1 and 2

On the board

S'pose u⃗\vec uu is a vector that describes displacement of an object.

u⃗=AB→\vec u = \overrightarrow{AB}u=AB w⃗=BC→\vec w = \overrightarrow{BC}w=BC v⃗=AC→=u⃗+w⃗\vec v = \overrightarrow{AC} = \vec u + \vec wv=AC=u+w

Define: the sum of vectors u⃗\vec uu and v⃗\vec vv, u⃗+v⃗\vec u + \vec vu+v, is the vector with same tail as u⃗\vec uu and head of v⃗\vec vv when tail of v⃗\vec vv is placed on tip of u⃗\vec uu.

Triangle law:

a⃗+b⃗=c⃗\vec a + \vec b = \vec ca+b=c

Parallelogram law:

u⃗+v⃗=v⃗+u⃗\vec u + \vec v = \vec v + \vec uu+v=v+u

Think of a vector as a move. Going from AAA to BBB and then from BBB to CCC leaves you in the same place as going straight from AAA to CCC. So “do u⃗\vec uu, then do w⃗\vec ww” is itself a move, and that move is what u⃗+w⃗\vec u + \vec wu+w means. To add any two vectors, slide the second so its tail sits on the tip of the first. The sum runs from the first tail to the last tip.

From your own notes on PDF page 2

Here's both constructions side by side:

Two things to read off it:

Both orange arrows are the same vector. Different constructions, same answer. That's u+v=v+u\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}u+v=v+u.

And θ\thetaθ only appears on the right side. That's the tail-to-tail placement, the one that feeds every formula. On the left, the triangle's interior angle at the tip is the supplement, π−θ\pi - \thetaπ−θ.

The parallelogram on the board is two triangle-law pictures glued along the diagonal. Go up the left side and across the top and you have done u⃗\vec uu then v⃗\vec vv. Go along the bottom and up the right side and you have done v⃗\vec vv then u⃗\vec uu. Both routes end at the same corner, which is the whole reason the order of addition does not matter. (The sum is drawn red here; your note calls it orange.)

What a test question on this looks like

A small diagram of several arrows, and you write a combination such as AB→+BC→\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC}AB+BC or CD→+DB→\overrightarrow{CD} + \overrightarrow{DB}CD+DB as a single vector, or you copy two given arrows and draw u⃗+v⃗\vec u + \vec vu+v and u⃗−v⃗\vec u - \vec vu−v from them. For the first kind, when the middle letter matches it cancels: AB→+BC→=AC→\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}AB+BC=AC.

Scalar multiples and subtraction

PDF pages 2 and 3

On the board

A scalar is a real number.

We stretch or compress vectors by multiplying by scalars. Ex.

We define

u⃗−v⃗=u⃗+(−1)v⃗=u⃗+−v⃗\vec u - \vec v = \vec u + (-1)\vec v = \vec u + -\vec vu−v=u+(−1)v=u+−v

u⃗−v⃗=r⃗=u⃗+−v⃗\vec u - \vec v = \vec r = \vec u + -\vec vu−v=r=u+−v

u⃗−v⃗\vec u - \vec vu−v is the vector from tip of v⃗\vec vv to tip of u⃗\vec uu, when u⃗\vec uu, v⃗\vec vv are placed with common tail.

Multiplying by a scalar ccc changes the length by the factor ∣c∣|c|∣c∣. A positive ccc keeps the direction and a negative ccc reverses it. c=0c = 0c=0 gives 0⃗\vec 00. Vectors that are scalar multiples of each other are parallel.

Subtraction is not a new operation. It is addition of the reversed vector. The second picture is the one to remember because it is fastest: put both tails together, and u⃗−v⃗\vec u - \vec vu−v is the arrow across the gap, pointing at u⃗\vec uu. Check it by reading the triangle as an addition: v⃗\vec vv and then r⃗\vec rr lands at the tip of u⃗\vec uu, so v⃗+r⃗=u⃗\vec v + \vec r = \vec uv+r=u.

Components: putting the tail at the origin

PDF pages 3 and 4

On the board

Coordinatize vectors by placing tails at origin.

In 2-d:

w⃗=u⃗=OP→=⟨5,2⟩=[52]\vec w = \vec u = \overrightarrow{OP} = \langle 5, 2\rangle = \begin{bmatrix}5\\2\end{bmatrix}w=u=OP=⟨5,2⟩=[52​]

OP→\overrightarrow{OP}OP is the position vector of w⃗\vec ww.

In 3-d:

v⃗=⟨2,−3,5⟩=[2−35]\vec v = \langle 2, -3, 5\rangle = \begin{bmatrix}2\\-3\\5\end{bmatrix}v=⟨2,−3,5⟩=​2−35​​
w⃗=AB→=⟨x2−x1,  y2−y1,  z2−z1⟩\vec w = \overrightarrow{AB} = \langle x_2 - x_1,\; y_2 - y_1,\; z_2 - z_1\ranglew=AB=⟨x2​−x1​,y2​−y1​,z2​−z1​⟩

Its position vector ends at P(x2−x1,  y2−y1,  z2−z1)P(x_2 - x_1,\; y_2 - y_1,\; z_2 - z_1)P(x2​−x1​,y2​−y1​,z2​−z1​).

Because a vector can be drawn anywhere, we are free to draw it starting at the origin. Then its tip lands on one particular point, and the coordinates of that point describe the vector completely. Those numbers are the components, written in angle brackets so they are not confused with a point.

In the 2-D picture the green arrow w⃗\vec ww runs from (−8,7)(-8, 7)(−8,7) to (−3,9)(-3, 9)(−3,9). That is 5 to the right and 2 up, the same as u⃗\vec uu, so w⃗=u⃗=⟨5,2⟩\vec w = \vec u = \langle 5, 2\ranglew=u=⟨5,2⟩ even though they sit in different places. That is where the rule for AB→\overrightarrow{AB}AB comes from: subtract the coordinates of the tail from those of the tip, “end minus start”.

On the board

Ex. A(5,−2,7)A(5, -2, 7)A(5,−2,7), B(3,8,1)B(3, 8, 1)B(3,8,1). Find the coordinatization of u⃗=AB→\vec u = \overrightarrow{AB}u=AB.

u⃗=⟨3−5,  8−(−2),  1−7⟩\vec u = \langle 3 - 5,\; 8 - (-2),\; 1 - 7\rangleu=⟨3−5,8−(−2),1−7⟩ u⃗=⟨−2,10,−6⟩\vec u = \langle -2, 10, -6\rangleu=⟨−2,10,−6⟩

Tail at OOO, tip at P(−2,10,−6)P(-2, 10, -6)P(−2,10,−6).

Length, and arithmetic by components

PDF pages 4 and 5

On the board

We denote the magnitude (length) of u⃗\vec uu by ∣u⃗∣|\vec u|∣u∣ or ∥u⃗∥\|\vec u\|∥u∥.

For u⃗=⟨−2,10,−6⟩\vec u = \langle -2, 10, -6\rangleu=⟨−2,10,−6⟩ from the example:

∣u⃗∣=(−2)2+102+36|\vec u| = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 10^2 + 36}∣u∣=(−2)2+102+36​ =140= \sqrt{140}=140​ =235= 2\sqrt{35}=235​

The length of u⃗=⟨a,b,c⟩\vec u = \langle a, b, c\rangleu=⟨a,b,c⟩ is

∣u⃗∣=a2+b2+c2|\vec u| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}∣u∣=a2+b2+c2​

We can add / subtract vectors by adding / subtracting component-wise:

⟨2,8⟩+⟨5,1⟩=⟨7,9⟩\langle 2, 8\rangle + \langle 5, 1\rangle = \langle 7, 9\rangle⟨2,8⟩+⟨5,1⟩=⟨7,9⟩

The dashed sides complete the parallelogram, so this is the parallelogram law with numbers on it.

u⃗=⟨2,8⟩\vec u = \langle 2, 8\rangleu=⟨2,8⟩ 3u⃗=⟨6,24⟩3\vec u = \langle 6, 24\rangle3u=⟨6,24⟩

A scalar multiplies every component.

Denote by VnV_nVn​ the set of all vectors in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn.

(n=3)(n = 3)(n=3): a vector in V3V_3V3​ is ⟨x,y,z⟩\langle x, y, z\rangle⟨x,y,z⟩; a point in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 is (x,y,z)(x, y, z)(x,y,z).

The length formula is the distance formula from 12.1 applied to the position vector: ∣u⃗∣|\vec u|∣u∣ is the distance from the origin to the point (a,b,c)(a, b, c)(a,b,c). In the worked line the 36 is (−6)2(-6)^2(−6)2, and 140=4⋅35=235\sqrt{140} = \sqrt{4 \cdot 35} = 2\sqrt{35}140​=4⋅35​=235​.

Adding component-wise agrees with the arrow picture. Doing ⟨2,8⟩\langle 2, 8\rangle⟨2,8⟩ and then ⟨5,1⟩\langle 5, 1\rangle⟨5,1⟩ moves you 2+52 + 52+5 across and 8+18 + 18+1 up in total.

What a test question on this looks like

Two vectors are given in components, say a⃗=⟨−2,5⟩\vec a = \langle -2, 5\ranglea=⟨−2,5⟩ and b⃗=⟨7,−1⟩\vec b = \langle 7, -1\rangleb=⟨7,−1⟩, and you find a⃗+b⃗\vec a + \vec ba+b, a combination like 4a⃗+2b⃗4\vec a + 2\vec b4a+2b,   ∣a⃗∣\;|\vec a|∣a∣ and ∣a⃗−b⃗∣|\vec a - \vec b|∣a−b∣. Do the vector arithmetic first and take the length last: ∣a⃗−b⃗∣|\vec a - \vec b|∣a−b∣ means subtract, then find the length of the result. It is not ∣a⃗∣−∣b⃗∣|\vec a| - |\vec b|∣a∣−∣b∣.

Properties of vectors

PDF pages 5 and 6

On the board

Properties of Vectors.

Let a⃗,b⃗,c⃗∈Vn\vec a, \vec b, \vec c \in V_na,b,c∈Vn​ (n=2,3)(n = 2, 3)(n=2,3). Let c,dc, dc,d be scalars (i.e. c,d∈Rc, d \in \mathbb{R}c,d∈R). Here 0⃗=⟨0,0⟩\vec 0 = \langle 0, 0\rangle0=⟨0,0⟩.

  1. a⃗+b⃗=b⃗+a⃗\vec a + \vec b = \vec b + \vec aa+b=b+a
  2. a⃗+0⃗=a⃗\vec a + \vec 0 = \vec aa+0=a
  3. (a⃗+b⃗)+c⃗=a⃗+(b⃗+c⃗)(\vec a + \vec b) + \vec c = \vec a + (\vec b + \vec c)(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)
  4. a⃗+(−a⃗)=0⃗\vec a + (-\vec a) = \vec 0a+(−a)=0
  1. c(a⃗+b⃗)=ca⃗+cb⃗c(\vec a + \vec b) = c\vec a + c\vec bc(a+b)=ca+cb
  2. (c+d)a⃗=ca⃗+da⃗(c + d)\vec a = c\vec a + d\vec a(c+d)a=ca+da
  3. (cd)a⃗=c(da⃗)=d(ca⃗)(cd)\vec a = c(d\vec a) = d(c\vec a)(cd)a=c(da)=d(ca)
  4. 1a⃗=a⃗1\vec a = \vec a1a=a

From your own notes on PDF page 5

The eight algebraic properties (Stewart p. 815), addition first:

a+b=b+aa+(b+c)=(a+b)+ca+0=aa+(−a)=0\begin{gathered}\mathbf a + \mathbf b = \mathbf b + \mathbf a\\ \mathbf a + (\mathbf b + \mathbf c) = (\mathbf a + \mathbf b) + \mathbf c\\ \mathbf a + \mathbf 0 = \mathbf a\\ \mathbf a + (-\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0\end{gathered}a+b=b+aa+(b+c)=(a+b)+ca+0=aa+(−a)=0​

Then scalars:

c(a+b)=ca+cb(c+d)a=ca+da(cd)a=c(da)1a=a\begin{gathered}c(\mathbf a + \mathbf b) = c\mathbf a + c\mathbf b\\ (c + d)\mathbf a = c\mathbf a + d\mathbf a\\ (cd)\mathbf a = c(d\mathbf a)\\ 1\mathbf a = \mathbf a\end{gathered}c(a+b)=ca+cb(c+d)a=ca+da(cd)a=c(da)1a=a​

These license ordinary algebra: expanding brackets, collecting terms, moving things across an equals sign.

None of these is surprising, and each one can be checked by writing the vectors in components and using the matching fact about real numbers. Their use is practical. They are the permission to simplify an expression like 2(a⃗+3b⃗)−5a⃗2(\vec a + 3\vec b) - 5\vec a2(a+3b)−5a exactly as you would with ordinary letters.

∣u⃗∣=1+16+9=26|\vec u| = \sqrt{1 + 16 + 9} = \sqrt{26}∣u∣=1+16+9​=26​

The standard basis vectors

PDF pages 6 and 7

On the board

The standard basis vectors in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3:

i⃗=⟨1,0,0⟩\vec i = \langle 1, 0, 0\ranglei=⟨1,0,0⟩ j⃗=⟨0,1,0⟩\vec j = \langle 0, 1, 0\ranglej​=⟨0,1,0⟩ k⃗=⟨0,0,1⟩\vec k = \langle 0, 0, 1\ranglek=⟨0,0,1⟩

Every vector in VnV_nVn​ (n=2,3)(n = 2, 3)(n=2,3) can be written as a sum of scalar multiples of i⃗,j⃗\vec i, \vec ji,j​ (when n=2n = 2n=2) or i⃗,j⃗,k⃗\vec i, \vec j, \vec ki,j​,k (n=3)(n = 3)(n=3),

i.e. a linear combination of i⃗,j⃗\vec i, \vec ji,j​ / i⃗,j⃗,k⃗\vec i, \vec j, \vec ki,j​,k.

Ex.

u⃗=⟨−4,3,8⟩\vec u = \langle -4, 3, 8\rangleu=⟨−4,3,8⟩ =−4⟨1,0,0⟩+3⟨0,1,0⟩+8⟨0,0,1⟩= -4\langle 1, 0, 0\rangle + 3\langle 0, 1, 0\rangle + 8\langle 0, 0, 1\rangle=−4⟨1,0,0⟩+3⟨0,1,0⟩+8⟨0,0,1⟩ =−4i⃗+3j⃗+8k⃗= -4\vec i + 3\vec j + 8\vec k=−4i+3j​+8k

Check, going the other way:

⟨−4,0,0⟩+⟨0,3,0⟩+⟨0,0,8⟩=⟨−4,3,8⟩\langle -4, 0, 0\rangle + \langle 0, 3, 0\rangle + \langle 0, 0, 8\rangle = \langle -4, 3, 8\rangle⟨−4,0,0⟩+⟨0,3,0⟩+⟨0,0,8⟩=⟨−4,3,8⟩

From your own notes on PDF page 6

The three unit vectors along the axes:

i=⟨1,0,0⟩j=⟨0,1,0⟩k=⟨0,0,1⟩\mathbf i = \langle 1, 0, 0\rangle \qquad \mathbf j = \langle 0, 1, 0\rangle \qquad \mathbf k = \langle 0, 0, 1\ranglei=⟨1,0,0⟩j=⟨0,1,0⟩k=⟨0,0,1⟩

Each has length 1, each points down a positive axis. (In 2D it's just i=⟨1,0⟩\mathbf i = \langle 1, 0\ranglei=⟨1,0⟩, j=⟨0,1⟩\mathbf j = \langle 0, 1\ranglej=⟨0,1⟩.)

The whole point: every vector decomposes into them:

⟨a1,a2,a3⟩=a1i+a2j+a3k\langle a_1, a_2, a_3\rangle = a_1\mathbf i + a_2\mathbf j + a_3\mathbf k⟨a1​,a2​,a3​⟩=a1​i+a2​j+a3​k

Why it works is just componentwise scaling and addition:

a1⟨1,0,0⟩+a2⟨0,1,0⟩+a3⟨0,0,1⟩=⟨a1,0,0⟩+⟨0,a2,0⟩+⟨0,0,a3⟩a_1\langle 1, 0, 0\rangle + a_2\langle 0, 1, 0\rangle + a_3\langle 0, 0, 1\rangle = \langle a_1, 0, 0\rangle + \langle 0, a_2, 0\rangle + \langle 0, 0, a_3\ranglea1​⟨1,0,0⟩+a2​⟨0,1,0⟩+a3​⟨0,0,1⟩=⟨a1​,0,0⟩+⟨0,a2​,0⟩+⟨0,0,a3​⟩

Concretely: ⟨3,−1,2⟩=3i−j+2k\langle 3, -1, 2\rangle = 3\mathbf i - \mathbf j + 2\mathbf k⟨3,−1,2⟩=3i−j+2k

Note the middle term. Coefficient −1-1−1 is written as just −j-\mathbf j−j, not −1j-1\mathbf j−1j.

From your own notes on PDF page 7: “why do we call it basis vector?”

Because everything else is built out of them. “Basis” in the ordinary sense: a foundation.

Two things have to be true for that word to be earned:

1. They reach everything. Any vector in 3-space can be written as a1i+a2j+a3ka_1\mathbf i + a_2\mathbf j + a_3\mathbf ka1​i+a2​j+a3​k. Nothing is out of reach: pick the right three coefficients and you can hit any arrow in space.

2. The way is unique. There's exactly one set of coefficients that works for a given vector. ⟨3,−1,2⟩\langle 3, -1, 2\rangle⟨3,−1,2⟩ is 3i−j+2k3\mathbf i - \mathbf j + 2\mathbf k3i−j+2k and nothing else. If there were two different ways to write the same vector, the components wouldn't be well-defined, and the word “the xxx-component” would be meaningless.

Together: reaches everything, exactly one way each. That's a basis.

The two notations say the same thing, and you should be able to switch on sight: the numbers in the angle brackets are the coefficients of i⃗\vec ii, j⃗\vec jj​, k⃗\vec kk, in that order. In the figure, the red path is the recipe −4i⃗+3j⃗+8k⃗-4\vec i + 3\vec j + 8\vec k−4i+3j​+8k followed one step at a time: 4 backward along xxx, 3 along yyy, 8 up. The blue arrow is where you end up.

What a test question on this looks like

The same arithmetic as before, with the vectors given in the other notation, for example a⃗=3i⃗−2j⃗+k⃗\vec a = 3\vec i - 2\vec j + \vec ka=3i−2j​+k and b⃗=5i⃗−4k⃗\vec b = 5\vec i - 4\vec kb=5i−4k. A missing letter means a zero component: b⃗=⟨5,0,−4⟩\vec b = \langle 5, 0, -4\rangleb=⟨5,0,−4⟩.

Unit vectors

PDF page 7

On the board

A unit vector is a vector of magnitude 1.

∣i⃗∣=∣j⃗∣=∣k⃗∣=1|\vec i| = |\vec j| = |\vec k| = 1∣i∣=∣j​∣=∣k∣=1

We want ∣cu⃗∣=1|c\vec u| = 1∣cu∣=1.

Take c=1∣u⃗∣c = \dfrac{1}{|\vec u|}c=∣u∣1​.

Then

∣cu⃗∣=c ∣u⃗∣=1∣u⃗∣⋅∣u⃗∣=1|c\vec u| = c\,|\vec u| = \frac{1}{|\vec u|}\cdot|\vec u| = 1∣cu∣=c∣u∣=∣u∣1​⋅∣u∣=1

Ex. Find a unit vector in the same direction as 4i⃗+3j⃗−k⃗4\vec i + 3\vec j - \vec k4i+3j​−k.

∣4i⃗+3j⃗−k⃗∣=42+32+(−1)2=26|4\vec i + 3\vec j - \vec k| = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{26}∣4i+3j​−k∣=42+32+(−1)2​=26​

A unit vector:

126⟨4,3,−1⟩=⟨426,  326,  −126⟩\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}\langle 4, 3, -1\rangle = \left\langle \frac{4}{\sqrt{26}},\; \frac{3}{\sqrt{26}},\; \frac{-1}{\sqrt{26}}\right\rangle26​1​⟨4,3,−1⟩=⟨26​4​,26​3​,26​−1​⟩

A unit vector carries a direction and nothing else, because its length is always 1. To get the unit vector pointing the same way as a given u⃗\vec uu, shrink or stretch u⃗\vec uu by exactly the factor that makes its length 1, and that factor is 1/∣u⃗∣1/|\vec u|1/∣u∣. Since ccc is positive the direction is unchanged. This only works when u⃗≠0⃗\vec u \ne \vec 0u=0, which is the note in brackets on the board.

You can always check an answer: (426)2+(326)2+(−126)2=16+9+126=1\left(\tfrac{4}{\sqrt{26}}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{26}}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{-1}{\sqrt{26}}\right)^2 = \tfrac{16 + 9 + 1}{26} = 1(26​4​)2+(26​3​)2+(26​−1​)2=2616+9+1​=1.

What a test question on this looks like

You are given a vector such as ⟨5,−12⟩\langle 5, -12\rangle⟨5,−12⟩ or 2i⃗−j⃗+2k⃗2\vec i - \vec j + 2\vec k2i−j​+2k and asked for the unit vector in the same direction. A common variation asks for a vector in that direction with a stated length, say 4. Find the unit vector first, then multiply it by 4.

Applications: force and velocity

PDF page 8

On the board

Applications.

Force is represented by vectors.

If several forces are acting on an object, the resultant force is the vector sum of the forces.

From your own notes on PDF page 8

The setup. A boat (or swimmer) points straight across the river, capable of 5 m/s in still water. The current carries everything downstream at 2 m/s.

Put i\mathbf ii downstream and j\mathbf jj across:

vboat=⟨0,5⟩vcurrent=⟨2,0⟩vresultant=⟨2,5⟩\mathbf v_{\text{boat}} = \langle 0, 5\rangle \qquad \mathbf v_{\text{current}} = \langle 2, 0\rangle \qquad \mathbf v_{\text{resultant}} = \langle 2, 5\ranglevboat​=⟨0,5⟩vcurrent​=⟨2,0⟩vresultant​=⟨2,5⟩

That's the green diagonal on his board: the parallelogram law, exactly the diagram from earlier. Both effects start at the same point; the sum is the diagonal.

Actual speed:

∣v∣=22+52=29≈5.39 m/s|\mathbf v| = \sqrt{2^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.39 \text{ m/s}∣v∣=22+52​=29​≈5.39 m/s

Actual direction, the angle off the intended straight-across heading:

tan⁡θ=25  ⟹  θ≈21.8∘ downstream\tan\theta = \frac{2}{5} \;\Longrightarrow\; \theta \approx 21.8^\circ \text{ downstream}tanθ=52​⟹θ≈21.8∘ downstream

So you aim due north and arrive northeast of where you wanted. The boat's heading and its course are different vectors.

Velocities add the same way forces do. The water moves the boat and the engine moves the boat, both at once, so the boat's true velocity over the ground is the vector sum. The same idea handles a plane in a crosswind.

What a test question on this looks like

A boat crossing a current, or a plane flying in a wind: you are given the speed and heading of the craft and the speed and direction of the water or air, and asked for the true speed and direction over the ground. The reverse version asks which way to steer so that you land directly across. Write each velocity in components, add, then find the length and the angle of the sum.

The 200 lb weight on two wires

PDF page 9

On the board

Ex. A 200 lb weight hangs by two wires. Find the tension in the wires.

Tension: the force required to hold the weight.

The weight is not moving, so the three forces on it add to zero: T⃗1+T⃗2+w⃗=0⃗\vec T_1 + \vec T_2 + \vec w = \vec 0T1​+T2​+w=0. One vector equation in the plane is two ordinary equations, one for the horizontal components and one for the vertical components. The green arrows are those components.

From your own notes on PDF page 9

Critical reading: those angles are measured from the ceiling (horizontal), not from vertical. That determines which trig function goes where.

Components. T1\mathbf T_1T1​ points up-left at 60∘60^\circ60∘ above horizontal; T2\mathbf T_2T2​ up-right at 45∘45^\circ45∘:

T1=∣T1∣ ⟨−cos⁡60∘,  sin⁡60∘⟩=∣T1∣⟨−12,  32⟩\mathbf T_1 = |\mathbf T_1|\,\langle -\cos 60^\circ,\; \sin 60^\circ\rangle = |\mathbf T_1|\left\langle -\tfrac12,\; \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right\rangleT1​=∣T1​∣⟨−cos60∘,sin60∘⟩=∣T1​∣⟨−21​,23​​⟩ T2=∣T2∣ ⟨cos⁡45∘,  sin⁡45∘⟩=∣T2∣⟨22,  22⟩\mathbf T_2 = |\mathbf T_2|\,\langle \cos 45^\circ,\; \sin 45^\circ\rangle = |\mathbf T_2|\left\langle \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2},\; \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right\rangleT2​=∣T2​∣⟨cos45∘,sin45∘⟩=∣T2​∣⟨22​​,22​​⟩ W=⟨0,−200⟩\mathbf W = \langle 0, -200\rangleW=⟨0,−200⟩

Two scalar equations. Horizontal components cancel; vertical components carry the weight:

−12∣T1∣+22∣T2∣=0-\tfrac12|\mathbf T_1| + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}|\mathbf T_2| = 0−21​∣T1​∣+22​​∣T2​∣=0 32∣T1∣+22∣T2∣=200\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}|\mathbf T_1| + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}|\mathbf T_2| = 20023​​∣T1​∣+22​​∣T2​∣=200

From the first: 22∣T2∣=12∣T1∣\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}|\mathbf T_2| = \dfrac12|\mathbf T_1|22​​∣T2​∣=21​∣T1​∣.

Substitute straight into the second. The whole second term becomes 12∣T1∣\tfrac12|\mathbf T_1|21​∣T1​∣:

32∣T1∣+12∣T1∣=200  ⟹  ∣T1∣⋅3+12=200\frac{\sqrt3}{2}|\mathbf T_1| + \frac12|\mathbf T_1| = 200 \;\Longrightarrow\; |\mathbf T_1|\cdot\frac{\sqrt3 + 1}{2} = 20023​​∣T1​∣+21​∣T1​∣=200⟹∣T1​∣⋅23​+1​=200

Answers.

∣T1∣=4003+1=200(3−1)≈146.4 lb|\mathbf T_1| = \frac{400}{\sqrt3 + 1} = 200(\sqrt3 - 1) \approx 146.4 \text{ lb}∣T1​∣=3​+1400​=200(3​−1)≈146.4 lb ∣T2∣=∣T1∣2=100(6−2)≈103.5 lb|\mathbf T_2| = \frac{|\mathbf T_1|}{\sqrt2} = 100(\sqrt6 - \sqrt2) \approx 103.5 \text{ lb}∣T2​∣=2​∣T1​∣​=100(6​−2​)≈103.5 lb

Two steps in the answers are worth seeing in full. To clear the surd from the denominator, multiply top and bottom by 3−1\sqrt3 - 13​−1:   4003+1⋅3−13−1=400(3−1)3−1=200(3−1)\;\dfrac{400}{\sqrt3 + 1}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3 - 1}{\sqrt3 - 1} = \dfrac{400(\sqrt3 - 1)}{3 - 1} = 200(\sqrt3 - 1)3​+1400​⋅3​−13​−1​=3−1400(3​−1)​=200(3​−1). And the first equation gives ∣T2∣=∣T1∣2|\mathbf T_2| = \dfrac{|\mathbf T_1|}{\sqrt2}∣T2​∣=2​∣T1​∣​ because 1/22/2=12\dfrac{1/2}{\sqrt2/2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}2​/21/2​=2​1​.

The steeper wire carries more of the load, 146.4 lb against 103.5 lb. The two tensions add up to more than 200 lb because part of each pull is sideways, and those sideways parts cancel each other instead of holding the weight up.

What a test question on this looks like

The same picture with different numbers: an object hangs from two ropes or wires that make given angles with the horizontal, and you find the tension in each one and its magnitude. The steps do not change: components of each tension, horizontal sum =0= 0=0, vertical sum === the weight, solve the two equations. If a mass is given in kg, the weight is mgmgmg with g=9.8g = 9.8g=9.8 m/s².
